items.stem:
Read the following newspaper editorial ("Our view") on a proposed curfew for under-16s.

OUR VIEW: A CURFEW WILL NOT MAKE OUR STREETS SAFER
The council's plan to ban under-16s from the town centre after 9 p.m. may sound tough. It is also lazy.
Police figures show that youth crime in the town fell by 12 per cent last year. The problem is not that teenagers are out; it is that there is nowhere for them to go. Two youth clubs have closed since 2022.
Treat young people as suspects and they will behave like them. Fund the clubs instead.

Identify the text type of this extract and explain how two of its conventions are used.
items.answer: It is a opinion column. Conventions: a by-line, a first-person argument on a topical issue, evidence and anecdote, a counterargument and a clear stance. In this text, for example: "The problem is not that teenagers are out; it is that there is nowhere for them to go." (antithesis) and the move from criticism to evidence to an alternative proposal, each chosen to suit the purpose and audience.

items.stem:
Read the following news report from a regional newspaper.

NEW STADIUM TO BRING 2,000 JOBS AND "A NEW HEART" TO RIVERSIDE
Councillors last night approved plans for a £300 million stadium on the Riverside estate, promising thousands of jobs and a revived town centre.
Council leader Priya Nair called the decision "historic". "Riverside has waited decades for investment," she said.
About 140 households will be relocated during construction. Local football fans celebrated outside the town hall.

Why might an editor choose to publish this story? Refer to news values.
items.answer: News values: impact (jobs, investment), proximity (a local estate), prominence (the council leader) and positivity – a story of regeneration.
items.markingKey: News values: impact (jobs, investment), proximity (a local estate), prominence (the council leader) and positivity – a story of regeneration. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Identify three news values in the stadium story.
items.answer: Impact (2,000 jobs, 140 homes); proximity (local estate); conflict (residents vs council); prominence (council leader).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "News values make journalism less objective."
items.answer: News values inevitably shape coverage; readers should be aware of them rather than expect total objectivity.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column by a Year 10 student in a school magazine in Melbourne.

Why I've Changed My Mind About Uniforms
In Year 7 I thought school uniform was a prison sentence in polyester. I wanted to wear my own clothes, my own style, my own identity.
Then I met Jonah. Jonah's family couldn't afford the brands everyone else wore. On mufti days he 'forgot' and wore his blazer anyway.
A uniform doesn't erase who we are. It erases the price tag.
Yes, the jumpers are itchy. Yes, the colour is a crime against fashion. But I'd rather be itchy than watch a friend hide.

Write a reply column (about 250 words) arguing that students should be allowed to wear their own clothes, responding to at least two of this writer's points.
items.answer: Indicative content: headline; clear counter-stance; addresses the Jonah argument (e.g. a clothing bank or plain dress code could solve inequality); self-expression and cost of uniforms; persuasive devices; conclusion.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: headline; clear counter-stance; addresses the Jonah argument (e.g. a clothing bank or plain dress code could solve inequality); self-expression and cost of uniforms; persuasive devices; conclusion. A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: "FAMILIES FACE EVICTION" and "A NEW HEART" frame the same story:
items.answer: negatively and positively
items.markingKey: B. Framing shapes meaning.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The criteria journalists use to decide what is newsworthy: impact, proximity, prominence, conflict, human interest, novelty and timeliness"?
items.answer: news values
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of news values.

items.stem: Distinguish between an editorial and a news report.
items.answer: A news report aims to inform with facts and attributed quotations; an editorial argues the newspaper's opinion using evidence and persuasive techniques.
items.markingKey: A news report aims to inform with facts and attributed quotations; an editorial argues the newspaper's opinion using evidence and persuasive techniques. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a reliable source and an unreliable source.
items.answer: A reliable source is transparent about authorship and evidence, accurate and corroborated; an unreliable source is anonymous, emotional and unverifiable.
items.markingKey: A reliable source is transparent about authorship and evidence, accurate and corroborated; an unreliable source is anonymous, emotional and unverifiable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between representation and reality.
items.answer: Representation is a constructed version of people or events; reality is more complex than any single representation.
items.markingKey: Representation is a constructed version of people or events; reality is more complex than any single representation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between soft news and hard news.
items.answer: Hard news covers urgent, important events (politics, disasters); soft news covers lighter human-interest stories (lifestyle, entertainment).
items.markingKey: Hard news covers urgent, important events (politics, disasters); soft news covers lighter human-interest stories (lifestyle, entertainment). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following newspaper editorial ("Our view") on a proposed curfew for under-16s.

OUR VIEW: A CURFEW WILL NOT MAKE OUR STREETS SAFER
The council's plan to ban under-16s from the town centre after 9 p.m. may sound tough. It is also lazy.
Police figures show that youth crime in the town fell by 12 per cent last year. The problem is not that teenagers are out; it is that there is nowhere for them to go. Two youth clubs have closed since 2022.
Treat young people as suspects and they will behave like them. Fund the clubs instead.

State the main purpose of the text and explain how one feature helps to achieve it.
items.answer: To persuade readers and councillors to reject the curfew and fund youth clubs instead. Supporting evidence: "The problem is not that teenagers are out; it is that there is nowhere for them to go." (antithesis) – the balanced sentence reframes the issue from behaviour to lack of facilities.
items.markingKey: To persuade readers and councillors to reject the curfew and fund youth clubs instead. Supporting evidence: "The problem is not that teenagers are out; it is that there is nowhere for them to go." (antithesis) – the balanced sentence reframes the issue from behaviour to lack of facilities. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following social media post that was widely shared.

🚨SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS🚨
My cousin works at the water company and says the city's tap water will be SWITCHED OFF for 3 DAYS from Monday!!! The government doesn't want you to know.
Fill your baths NOW. Buy bottled water while you still can.
Doctors are saying this is the worst crisis in 50 years. Wake up people!!!
#WaterCrisis #TheyAreLying

How does this text try to make readers believe it? Evaluate how reliable it is.
items.answer: Red flags: an anonymous second-hand source ("My cousin works at the water company"); vague authorities ("Doctors are saying"); urgency and fear ("SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS", "NOW"); conspiracy framing ("The government doesn't want you to know"); capital letters and multiple exclamation marks; no date, link or official source.
items.markingKey: Red flags: an anonymous second-hand source ("My cousin works at the water company"); vague authorities ("Doctors are saying"); urgency and fear ("SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS", "NOW"); conspiracy framing ("The government doesn't want you to know"); capital letters and multiple exclamation marks; no date, link or official source. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Text A: news report from a regional newspaper.

NEW STADIUM TO BRING 2,000 JOBS AND "A NEW HEART" TO RIVERSIDE
Councillors last night approved plans for a £300 million stadium on the Riverside estate, promising thousands of jobs and a revived town centre.
Council leader Priya Nair called the decision "historic". "Riverside has waited decades for investment," she said.
About 140 households will be relocated during construction. Local football fans celebrated outside the town hall.

Text B: news report from a community news website.

FAMILIES FACE EVICTION AS COUNCIL BACKS £300M STADIUM
One hundred and forty families on the Riverside estate could lose their homes after councillors voted last night to build a stadium on the site.
"My children were born in this flat," said Joan Mensah, 62, who has lived on the estate for thirty years. "Nobody asked us."
The council claims the project will create 2,000 jobs. Campaigners say most will be temporary.

Identify ONE similarity and ONE difference between the two texts, supporting each with a reference to both texts.
items.answer: Similarity: both report the same core facts – the vote, the £300m cost, 2,000 jobs and 140 households. Difference: Text A frames the decision as regeneration through the council leader's voice, whereas Text B frames it as eviction through a resident's voice.
items.markingKey: Similarity: both report the same core facts – the vote, the £300m cost, 2,000 jobs and 140 households. Difference: Text A frames the decision as regeneration through the council leader's voice, whereas Text B frames it as eviction through a resident's voice. One mark for each valid, supported point; credit other valid comparisons.

items.stem: Write a two-sentence concession and rebuttal for an editorial supporting longer school holidays.
items.answer: E.g. "Critics argue that longer holidays harm learning. Yet research shows rested students return more focused, and holidays offer time for family, work and rest." Credit concession and rebuttal.

items.stem: "Fact-checking is only for journalists." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Everyone can check claims using lateral reading, official sources and reverse image searches before sharing.
items.markingKey: Everyone can check claims using lateral reading, official sources and reverse image searches before sharing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Completely unbiased journalism is impossible."
items.answer: Total neutrality is impossible because selection is unavoidable, but fairness and balance are realistic goals.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: every report involves selection; journalists have perspectives. Arguments against: professional standards reduce bias; balance and attribution are achievable. Supported judgement: Total neutrality is impossible because selection is unavoidable, but fairness and balance are realistic goals.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "News values make journalism less objective."
items.answer: News values inevitably shape coverage; readers should be aware of them rather than expect total objectivity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they favour drama and conflict; they shape which stories are told. Arguments against: they help readers find relevant stories; they are necessary choices, not lies.
